text.reference:
Grain Pier Faces a Long Wait
By Rosalind Tiernan
Letters to this paper have run strongly in favour of
keeping the pier, though few of the writers offer to pay
for it. One retired pilot recalled tying up alongside it in
fog, guided only by the smell of the malt sheds.
The quay has changed hands four times since the war,
and each owner has left behind a plan that came to
nothing. A folder of drawings for a ferry terminal still sits
in the commission's basement, its corners nibbled by
mice.
Younger residents see it differently. A petition from the
sixth-form college asks for a rowing club and a small
boatyard, arguing that a working pier would keep skills
in the town that a market stall never could.
What the town lacks is not ideas but a season long
enough to pay for them. The hotels on the front open at
Easter and shutter by the first gales, and their owners are
wary of promises about year-round trade.
Whatever is decided, the engineers agree on one thing:
the longer the timber sits untreated, the less there will be
to argue over. Each winter takes a little more of the outer
deck, and the gulls have already moved in.
Estimated cost: 725,000 pounds
Opinion on the quay
Repairs would take the better part of two summers. The
surveyor told the meeting that the piles nearest the
channel were sound, but that the deck had softened
along much of its length and could not safely carry a
vehicle.
The commission will publish its findings after a further
round of soundings, and has promised a public meeting
before any contract is signed. Until then the gates on the
pier will stay locked and the warning notices will remain.
The harbour commission met on Tuesday to weigh the
future of the old grain pier, which has stood idle since
the last barge left. Members heard from engineers,
fishermen and a delegation of residents from the
terraces above the quay, most of whom wanted the
timber kept.
Traders along the waterfront were divided. Some saw a
market hall on the pier as the only way to bring visitors
down the hill, while others feared that a long closure of
the quay road would cost them a season of custom.
A smaller group argued for doing nothing at all. The
tide, they said, would settle the question eventually, and
the money would be better spent on the lifeboat station,
whose slipway has needed attention for some years.
